difficultyRationale: Requires rejecting the DI-equals-DIP misconception the issue specifically calls out, in favor of a refactor that actually changes the direction of the source dependency.
explanation: DIP is satisfied when the high-level module's own dependency is on an abstraction it defines, and the low-level detail is what adapts to that abstraction — not merely when a concrete dependency arrives from outside via a framework. Injecting the concrete `SmtpEmailSender` fixes testability but not the dependency direction; the correct refactor introduces an `OrderNotifier` abstraction that `OrderService` owns and depends on, with the SMTP detail implementing it.

options.text: Add a constructor parameter `SmtpEmailSender emailSender` to `OrderService` and let Spring `@Autowired`-inject it, removing the `new SmtpEmailSender(...)` call.
options.explanation: This is dependency injection without dependency inversion: `OrderService` now receives its `SmtpEmailSender` from outside instead of constructing it, which helps testability, but it still depends directly on the concrete SMTP class and its constructor shape — exactly the conflation the team wanted to avoid.

options.text: Keep the direct `new SmtpEmailSender(...)` call, but move it into a `@PostConstruct` initializer method annotated on `OrderService` so the SMTP client is constructed once when the Spring bean is created and cached in a field, instead of being allocated fresh on every single `placeOrder` invocation, which also avoids repeatedly opening a new socket connection to `smtp.internal:587`.
options.explanation: This changes when the concrete class is constructed, not what `OrderService` depends on; `OrderService` still has a hard, compiled-in dependency on `SmtpEmailSender`, so the coupling DIP addresses is unchanged.

options.text: Mark `SmtpEmailSender` with `@Primary` so Spring prefers it automatically if another email sender bean is ever added.
options.explanation: `@Primary` resolves ambiguity between multiple beans of the same type at injection time; it has no effect on whether `OrderService` depends on a concrete class or an abstraction, so it doesn't touch the DIP concern at all.

options.text: Define an `OrderNotifier` abstraction (owned alongside `OrderService`, in the order/domain package) with a method like `notifyOrderConfirmed(Order order)`; have `OrderService` depend only on `OrderNotifier`, injected through its constructor, and move the SMTP-specific code into an `SmtpOrderNotifier implements OrderNotifier` class that lives in an infrastructure package.
options.explanation: Correct. `OrderService`, the high-level module, now depends only on an abstraction it owns the definition of; the low-level SMTP detail depends on that abstraction instead of `OrderService` depending on the SMTP detail, which is the inversion DIP describes.
